Yale University graduate Jordan Mechner took his video camera to a parking lot and persuaded his younger brother, David, to leap and scramble around grass verges and brick walls. Mechner developed the footage into the tiny digital hero of his latest videogame creation, the follow-up to a popular martial arts game he had cooked up on his dorm room Apple Il computer. Computer game distributor Brøderbund Software released Prince of Persia in 1989, and, over the next two decades, the unnamed prince went on to further adventures in a trilogy of Ubisoft games that sold more than 14 million copies. In 2004, Mechner brought a two-minute demo reel of Prince of Persia game action to the attention of producer Jerry Bruckheimer and was engaged as screenwriter and executive producer of a feature film adaptation. Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time - written by Boaz Yakin, Doug Miro and Carlo Bernard, from Mechner's story - identifies the prince as Dastan (Jake Gyllenhaal), a wily street urchin adopted by Persian King Sharaman (Ronald Pickup) and raised as an equal amongst the king's natural offspring. Sharaman's ambitious brother, Nizam (Ben Kingsley), persuades Dastan and his brothers to attack Alamut, an ancient sacred city where the Princess Tamina (Gemma Arterton) guards an enchanted dagger that has the power to turn back time. by filmmaker Ridley Scott for his Crusader epic, Kingdom of Heaven. "The Orientalists were a group of Victorian painters that depicted Arabian and Middle Eastern settings in a very romantic way, noted visual effects supervisor Tom Wood, who joined the production, together with visual effects producer Sharon Lark, in early 2008.iIt was a very fanciful depiction of 6th-century Persia, with beautiful girls in slave markets, men smoking weird substances, fantastic Arabic architecture and crumbling statues in the desert, most often backlit." Production designer Wolf Kroeger combined locations in Morocco with soundstage sets and digital set extensions, mapped out using 3D models developed with previsualization supervisor Martin Chamney at Nvizage.iWe used previz to make adjustments for budget and scale considerations," stated Wood. We changed that to a night attack with Dastan leading a small group of men through a side door while the main Persian attack happened in the background. That was easier to shoot, and helped show our hero as rebellious and also concerned about indiscriminately killing his way into Alamuti Kroger's sets filled nine soundstages at Pinewood Studios and a variety of Moroccan locales, including a large portion of the mountain village of Tamesloht, 14 • CINEFEX 123 ruckheimer encouraged director Mike Newell to paint a broad and exotic canvas for the film, taking inspiration from art reference gathered outside Marrakech, which represented street-level scenes in Alamut. Known as 'dagger time,' the effect required experimentation to arrive at an intelligible and visually compelling time reversal. 'Jerry Bruckheimer was very clear he didn't want to just see the film running backwards," remarked Tom Wood. "There were various descriptions in the script of the world warping around characters, and we looked at doing versions of that, but it became confusing. We discovered that the viewer had to experience the effect through a character's eyes to appreciate what was going on. Nvizage arrived at a previsualization depicting Dastan wrenched from his own body to observe the rewind as a third-person 'Ghost Dastan.' Double Negative developed the effect using impressionistic time dilation effects derived from photographic elements.iI wanted to create long, 30-second motion blurs around the characters," said Wood. "The camera traveled around these volumetric streams with the characters, created using Double Negative's 'event capture' system, which they'd used for the freefall sequence in Quantum of Solace. For our production, that involved surrounding the scene with an array of Arri 435 cameras running at 48 frames per second, using a 90-degree shutter to capture as much information as sharply as possible. From that footage, Double Negative reconstructed a virtual camera that could travel along the arc of the array. We then created long exposure trails from the photographic elements by taking 30 seconds of action and streaking it through frame. As characters moved backward through time, they disturbed the streaks, which dissipated as the rewind ended, and then everything resumed moving forward again. To develop rewind concepts, Double Negative created conceptual paintings and long-exposure still photography tests, and used event capture technoloqy to hone three-dimensional reproductions of characters. 'We first roughly rotoscoped each character from each camera in the arrayiexplained Double Negative visual effects supervisor Michael Ellis. 'That gave us nine pieces of footage for each shot, and nine pieces of roto for each character. We used the roto to carve a basic 3D form for each character. This was like a rough lump of clay, but with each camera that we more fanciful effect, derived from the videogame, involved characters' use of the Dagger of Time to freeze time and rewind action by 30 added we could whittle down the core element.
